script.opening: "I don’t really know why I’m still like this. I’ve been taking the tablets exactly as told, I’ve cut out everything — sugar, bread, the lot — and I’m drinking gallons of water and weeing constantly and STILL losing weight. My family keep saying I must be sneaking food, that I brought this on myself eating badly. But honestly, doc, I barely eat now and it’s getting worse, not better."

facts.text: If explored: slim build, unintentional 6 kg loss, marked polydipsia and polyuria, escalating glucose despite genuine adherence and dietary restriction, dual oral agents failing fast. If asked specifically: some nausea, occasional "fruity" breath he’s noticed, more tired than ever. This is insulin deficiency, not insulin resistance.

38, BMI 23, no family history of type 2, preceding viral illness, rapid failure of oral therapy — the classic profile of LADA / late-onset type 1, mislabelled type 2 on the HbA1c alone. Ketones and GAD antibodies / C-peptide were never checked.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the BLAME. His family (and, he felt, the clinician who diagnosed him) framed this as his fault for "eating wrong". He has internalised deep shame and is half-starving himself trying to "fix" what he believes he caused. He rings as much for absolution as for help — to find out whether he really did this to himself.

If reached: he’s stopped eating with his family to avoid the comments, is frightened by the weight loss but assumes it means he’s "still doing something wrong." No one has told him this might not be type 2 at all.

Officially: stronger tablets / to know why the tablets aren’t working. Actually: to be told this is not his fault, to understand what is really happening, and to be made safe — he is closer to DKA than anyone has recognised.

ice.ideas: His type 2 diabetes is "out of control" because he’s failed to eat well enough — the tablets should work and aren’t, so it must be him.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — shame and self-blame absorbed from family/diagnosis ("you did this by eating wrong"); he is starving himself to atone and frightened by relentless weight loss.
ice.expectations: Stronger medication or an explanation. What he actually needs: recognition that this is likely NOT type 2 (LADA/type 1), urgent safety assessment for DKA, and the lifting of misplaced blame.

cues: Slim, young, weight-losing, oral agents failing fast — the profile that should trigger "is this really type 2?"
"Fruity breath", nausea, gallons of thirst, escalating sugars — possible evolving DKA; assess urgency now.
"My family say I brought this on myself" — the blame is central; lifting it is half the consultation.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the diagnosis is likely WRONG: a slim 38-year-old with weight loss, marked osmotic symptoms, no FH of T2DM, a viral prodrome and rapid failure of dual oral therapy fits autoimmune diabetes (LADA / late-onset type 1), not type 2 — and that the current track is wrong: a sulfonylurea works by making the beta cells release insulin, so it fails as those cells are destroyed and only delays the insulin he needs, while diet restriction in insulin deficiency worsens catabolism and ketosis (and, with gliclazide, risks hypoglycaemia)

Assesses acute safety FIRST: checks for DKA features (thirst, polyuria, weight loss, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, drowsiness, rapid breathing) and arranges urgent capillary glucose and blood ketone testing — same-day (within the hour), with a low threshold for acute admission (JBDS-IP defines DKA by ketonaemia of 3.0 mmol/L or more, glucose above 11.0 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3)

Acts on the suspected type 1/LADA appropriately: urgent same-day diabetes specialist contact, does NOT simply add another oral agent or tell him to restrict further; recognises he likely needs insulin and that delay risks DKA

Plans the work-up proportionately: ketones now; NICE NG17 advises NOT measuring C-peptide or antibodies routinely, but considering them when the type is uncertain or features are atypical — as here, where the label is disputed — while making clear insulin and safety are never delayed waiting for the results

Explicitly LIFTS the blame: this is an autoimmune condition where the body stops making insulin — it is NOT caused by eating badly and NOT his fault; the weight loss and failing tablets are the disease, not his weakness; corrects the family’s narrative directly
Hears the shame and self-starvation and addresses it as central, not incidental; does not reinforce the "try harder with diet" framing that is harming him
Delivers the reframe with compassion: relief that there IS an explanation and it isn’t his fault, balanced with honest seriousness about needing urgent assessment today

Safety-nets robustly: precise DKA red flags → 999/A&E (vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, breathlessness); same-day specialist/acute pathway confirmed; tells him NOT to keep restricting food; a defined who-rings-whom plan and follow-up

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang, because what you’re describing tells me something important: the tablets aren’t failing because of anything you’re doing wrong. In someone slim, your age, losing weight this fast with tablets that should work — I don’t think this is type 2 diabetes at all. I think it may have been labelled wrongly."

"So let me say this as clearly as I can, because I think you’ve been carrying it heavily: you did NOT do this by eating badly. The kind of diabetes I’m now thinking of is where the body’s own immune system stops it making insulin — nobody causes it with bread or sugar. The weight loss and the thirst aren’t you failing; they’re the illness. Your family mean well, but they’ve got this wrong, and so, I’m sorry to say, did the first diagnosis."

"Before anything else I need to check how safe you are today. The thirst, the weight loss, the fruity smell you noticed, any nausea — together those can mean your body is running short of insulin and tipping into something we treat urgently. I need you to get a blood test today, and I’m going to talk to the diabetes team straight away."

"And please — stop restricting your food. I know you’ve been trying to fix this by eating less and less, but if your body can’t make insulin, starving yourself makes it more dangerous, not less. This was never a willpower problem. You can eat normally."

"What you most likely need isn’t a stronger tablet — it’s insulin, the thing your body has stopped making, and the specialist team will start that properly. The specialists may also do some blood tests to help confirm the type, because your label is in doubt, but we don’t wait on those to keep you safe."

"Here’s what matters most before I get you that appointment: if you start vomiting, get tummy pain, feel drowsy or your breathing speeds up — that’s 999 or A&E immediately, don’t wait. I’ll ring you back within the hour to confirm the plan and make sure you’ve been seen. You came in thinking you’d failed. You haven’t — you were mislabelled, and now we’re going to put it right."

f.learning: The classic SCA diabetes trap: a slim, young adult labelled "type 2" on the HbA1c alone who is actually insulin-deficient — LADA / late-onset type 1. The flags are unmistakable once looked for: slim build, unintentional weight loss, marked osmotic symptoms, no family history of T2DM, a viral prodrome, and rapid failure of oral agents. The danger is twofold: ongoing wrong treatment (a sulfonylurea that depends on the beta cells he is losing, plus dietary restriction that worsens catabolism and ketosis) and an evolving DKA that no one has screened for. Assess acute safety first (ketones, DKA features, low threshold to admit), get urgent specialist input, consider antibodies/C-peptide because the type is uncertain (NICE NG17: not routine, but considered when the type is in doubt) without delaying safety, and recognise he needs insulin not stronger tablets. The examinable hidden agenda is the blame: family and the initial diagnosis framed it as his dietary fault, and he is shamefully starving himself to atone. Lift that blame explicitly — autoimmune diabetes is not caused by eating badly — stop the self-starvation, and deliver the reframe with both compassion and urgency.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG17 · NICE NG28 (updated February 2026) · JBDS-IP DKA guideline · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (diabetes)
knowledge.summary: A slim adult under 50, losing weight, with marked osmotic symptoms and oral treatment failing within months, has type 1 diabetes (including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) until proven otherwise. The first task is safety: ketones and same-day specialist care.

points.t: NICE NG17: type 1 diabetes is diagnosed clinically; typical features include ketosis, rapid weight loss, age under 50, BMI below 25 and personal or family history of autoimmune disease. HbA1c confirms diabetes but not its type.

NICE NG17: do not measure C-peptide or antibodies routinely; consider them when the type is uncertain or features are atypical. Here they help settle a disputed label, but insulin must never wait for the results.

Thirst, polyuria, weight loss, nausea, ketotic breath, abdominal pain, vomiting, rapid breathing or drowsiness suggest ketosis. JBDS-IP defines DKA by ketonaemia of 3.0 mmol/L or more (or significant ketonuria), glucose above 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or breathlessness means emergency admission.

Suspected new type 1 diabetes with ketosis symptoms needs capillary glucose and blood ketones today and same-day discussion with the diabetes team or acute medicine. Do not add another oral agent or tighten the diet; insulin is the likely treatment.

Food restriction in insulin deficiency worsens catabolism and ketosis. Tell him clearly to eat normally and keep drinking sugar-free fluids. An SGLT2 inhibitor is not a fix here — it raises DKA risk in insulin deficiency (BNF).

Group 1: notify the DVLA if insulin treatment will last more than 3 months; check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; if it is 5.0 mmol/L or less, eat a snack first; do not drive if glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L. Group 2 has stricter rules.
NICE NG17: structured education (for example DAFNE) 6–12 months after diagnosis, offer of continuous glucose monitoring, and ongoing specialist care.

model.text: Hello Mr Wójcik, it’s Dr Lee. I’ve read your message. Before we start — are you somewhere you can talk, and how are you feeling right this minute?
model.why: Checks setting and immediate wellbeing on the phone

model.text: I’m at home. I don’t get it. I take the tablets exactly as told, I’ve cut out sugar, bread, everything. I’m drinking gallons, weeing all the time and still losing weight. My family say I must be sneaking food. But I barely eat now.
Thank you — that’s really clear, and I believe you. I want to ask some questions to understand what’s going on, because what you describe matters. Then we’ll agree what to do today. All right?
model.why: Believes him explicitly and sets an agenda

model.text: Okay.
How much weight have you lost, and over how long?
About six kilos since diagnosis. Four months. I wasn’t big to start with.
Have you had any nausea or vomiting, tummy pain, or noticed a sweet or fruity smell on your breath? Any breathlessness or feeling drowsy?
Bit sick in the mornings. I’ve noticed my breath smells funny, sort of fruity. No vomiting. Tired all the time.
Do you have a glucose meter at home? Any recent readings?
The nurse gave me one. It says 19, 22. Sometimes just ‘high’.
Does anyone in your family have diabetes, or conditions like thyroid disease or coeliac disease? And were you unwell before you were diagnosed?
model.why: Tests the type 1 hypothesis: family history, autoimmunity, viral prodrome

model.text: No, nobody in the family has diabetes. I had a bad virus just before all this started.
You mentioned your family say you must be sneaking food. How has that been for you?
Awful. I don’t eat with them anymore. When I was diagnosed I felt like it was my fault — eating wrong. So I stopped eating. And it’s still getting worse. So it must be me.
So you’ve been punishing yourself for something you believe you caused. What were you hoping I’d do today?
model.why: Names the self-blame and asks his expectation

model.text: Stronger tablets, I suppose. Or tell me what I’m doing wrong.

I’m going to be very clear: you are not doing anything wrong. Someone slim, your age, losing weight this fast, with sugars climbing on two tablets — I don’t think this is type 2 diabetes. I think it’s a different kind, where the immune system stops the body making insulin. It’s not caused by food. Nobody gets it from bread or sugar.
model.why: Reframes the diagnosis and lifts the blame explicitly

model.text: (Silence.) So it wasn’t me?
It wasn’t you. The weight loss and the thirst are the illness, not you failing. Your family meant well, but they had it wrong — and I’m sorry to say the first label was probably wrong too.
model.why: Repeats the absolution and acknowledges the mislabelling honestly

model.text: I don’t know whether to laugh or cry.

Either is fine. But the pear-drop smell and the sickness worry me today. They can mean your body is short of insulin and making ketones, which can tip into a serious condition called DKA. I need you checked today — a finger-prick test for sugar and ketones.
model.why: Prioritises acute safety: possible evolving DKA

model.text: Today? I feel all right, just tired.

I’d like you at the surgery within the hour. The nurse will check your sugar and ketones and I’ll speak to the hospital diabetes team straight away. If the ketones are raised, you’ll go to hospital today, and they’ll most likely start insulin. Can someone drive you?
model.why: Same-day ketone testing and specialist contact; arranges safe transport

model.text: Someone at home can. Insulin — that’s injections?

Yes. It replaces what your body has stopped making. The team will teach you everything, and people do very well on it. There’s also a blood test for antibodies that can confirm the type, but we won’t wait for that to treat you.
model.why: Explains insulin and confirmatory tests without delaying treatment

model.text: I drive for work. Will I lose my licence?

Not for having diabetes. On insulin there are DVLA rules — checking your sugar before and during driving, and telling them if it’s long term — and the team will go through them. For today, please don’t drive yourself.
model.why: Accurate DVLA reassurance and same-day driving advice

model.text: Okay.
And from now, please eat normally. Cutting food makes this more dangerous, not less. Keep drinking water. Don’t change your tablets yourself until the team sees you.
model.why: Stops self-starvation and gives interim medicines advice

model.text: Eat normally. Right.

If before you get here you start vomiting, get tummy pain, feel drowsy or your breathing speeds up, call 999 — don’t wait for us. I’ll ring the nurse now so she’s expecting you, and I’ll call you back this afternoon with the plan.
model.why: Precise DKA safety-net and a defined call-back

model.text: Thank you. Nobody’s said any of this before.
Can you tell me what you’re going to do now, and what you’ll tell your family tonight?
Get a lift in now. Finger-prick test. Maybe hospital, probably insulin. Eat normally. 999 if I’m sick or drowsy. And I’ll tell them it’s not my fault — it’s my immune system.

social.t: Relatives have framed the illness as his fault; he now eats alone and restricts food. Give him words to explain autoimmune diabetes at home and offer to see him with his wife.
He drives for work. Time off for admission and insulin starting, and a fit note if needed; later, a plan for glucose checks around driving.

legal.t: Group 1: notify if insulin will be needed for more than 3 months; glucose check within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; snack first at 5.0 mmol/L or less; do not drive below 4.0 mmol/L. Group 2 (lorry, bus) has additional requirements. Ask what he drives.
Insulin-treated diabetes may meet the definition of disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work, such as breaks for glucose checks and injections.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and the professional duty of candour: explain honestly that the original classification was probably wrong, without blaming colleagues, and record the revised working diagnosis and the plan.
A slim adult coded as type 2 on HbA1c alone, with no ketone check, is a learning opportunity for the practice: review how diabetes type is assigned at diagnosis.

community.t: Diabetes UK and Breakthrough T1D for newly diagnosed adults; structured education (for example DAFNE) via the diabetes team; peer support groups for adults diagnosed with type 1 later in life.

playbook.diagnosis: Probable autoimmune (type 1) diabetes, possibly latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, misclassified as type 2: slim, 38, 6 kg weight loss, marked osmotic symptoms, rapid failure of metformin and gliclazide, no family history of type 2 diabetes, preceding viral illness. Symptoms suggest ketosis — DKA must be excluded today.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “I think your immune system has damaged the cells that make insulin. That’s a different kind of diabetes from the one you were told, and it isn’t caused by food. Without enough insulin your body burns itself for fuel — that’s the weight loss and the funny-smelling breath — and the fix is insulin.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been punishing yourself for something you didn’t cause. This isn’t about eating wrong, and stronger tablets won’t help — insulin will.”
management.psychosocial: Stop the food restriction today; give him the words for his family; offer a joint conversation with a family member if he wishes; address work and driving.
sharedPlan: Seen within the hour: capillary glucose and blood ketones; same-day diabetes team or acute medicine discussion
Insulin via the specialist team; GAD antibodies and C-peptide if the type remains uncertain (NICE NG17) — not delaying treatment
Eat normally, drink sugar-free fluids, no driving today, no self-adjustment of tablets
safetyNet: Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or rapid breathing — 999
Nurse pre-warned; GP call-back this afternoon; follow-up once the specialist plan is in place

pitfalls.intro: The trap is in the title of his records: “type 2”. The station is failed by treating the label and passed by treating the patient — a slim young man in insulin deficiency who thinks it is his fault.

items.fail: Adding a third oral agent or advising stricter carbohydrate restriction.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG17 features point to type 1; insulin, not more tablets, is needed.
items.fix: Say you doubt the type 2 label and arrange same-day specialist input.

items.fail: Missing the ketotic breath and nausea.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Evolving DKA must be excluded today.
items.fix: Ask directly about vomiting, abdominal pain, breath and drowsiness; check ketones within the hour.

items.fail: Waiting for GAD antibodies before acting.
items.why: Antibodies help classify, but NICE NG17 treats type 1 as a clinical diagnosis; delay risks DKA.
items.fix: “We’ll do the antibody test, but we won’t wait for it to treat you.”

items.fail: Letting “my family say I’m sneaking food” pass.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The blame is the hidden agenda and is driving self-starvation.
items.fix: Say explicitly: “You didn’t cause this. It’s your immune system, not food.”

items.fail: Delivering the new diagnosis without acknowledging the earlier mislabelling.
items.why: He will not trust the new plan if the old one is defended.
items.fix: Be honest and non-blaming: “I think the first label was probably wrong.”

items.fail: Vague safety-netting and letting him drive himself in.
items.why: Non-specific advice in possible DKA is unsafe.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, arrange a driver, pre-warn the nurse and book a call-back.

SCA_MODELS.text: Someone at home can. Insulin — that’s injections?

Yes. It replaces what your body has stopped making. The team will teach you everything, and people do very well on it. There’s also a blood test for antibodies that can confirm the type, but we won’t wait for that to treat you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains insulin and confirmatory tests without delaying treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: I drive for work. Will I lose my licence?

Not for having diabetes. On insulin there are DVLA rules — checking your sugar before and during driving, and telling them if it’s long term — and the team will go through them. For today, please don’t drive yourself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate DVLA reassurance and same-day driving advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
And from now, please eat normally. Cutting food makes this more dangerous, not less. Keep drinking water. Don’t change your tablets yourself until the team sees you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Stops self-starvation and gives interim medicines advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Eat normally. Right.

If before you get here you start vomiting, get tummy pain, feel drowsy or your breathing speeds up, call 999 — don’t wait for us. I’ll ring the nurse now so she’s expecting you, and I’ll call you back this afternoon with the plan.
SCA_MODELS.why: Precise DKA safety-net and a defined call-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. Nobody’s said any of this before.
Can you tell me what you’re going to do now, and what you’ll tell your family tonight?
Get a lift in now. Finger-prick test. Maybe hospital, probably insulin. Eat normally. 999 if I’m sick or drowsy. And I’ll tell them it’s not my fault — it’s my immune system.

SCA_STEM.name: Tomasz Wójcik
SCA_STEM.recent: BMI 23 at diagnosis. No family history of type 2 diabetes recorded. No ketone, GAD antibody or C-peptide results on file. Weight today by his report about 6 kg lower than at diagnosis.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: “sugars still high, tablets not working”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG17 · NICE NG28 (updated February 2026) · JBDS-IP DKA guideline · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (diabetes)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A slim adult under 50, losing weight, with marked osmotic symptoms and oral treatment failing within months, has type 1 diabetes (including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) until proven otherwise. The first task is safety: ketones and same-day specialist care.

points.t: NICE NG17: type 1 diabetes is diagnosed clinically; typical features include ketosis, rapid weight loss, age under 50, BMI below 25 and personal or family history of autoimmune disease. HbA1c confirms diabetes but not its type.

NICE NG17: do not measure C-peptide or antibodies routinely; consider them when the type is uncertain or features are atypical. Here they help settle a disputed label, but insulin must never wait for the results.

Thirst, polyuria, weight loss, nausea, ketotic breath, abdominal pain, vomiting, rapid breathing or drowsiness suggest ketosis. JBDS-IP defines DKA by ketonaemia of 3.0 mmol/L or more (or significant ketonuria), glucose above 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or breathlessness means emergency admission.

Suspected new type 1 diabetes with ketosis symptoms needs capillary glucose and blood ketones today and same-day discussion with the diabetes team or acute medicine. Do not add another oral agent or tighten the diet; insulin is the likely treatment.

Food restriction in insulin deficiency worsens catabolism and ketosis. Tell him clearly to eat normally and keep drinking sugar-free fluids. An SGLT2 inhibitor is not a fix here — it raises DKA risk in insulin deficiency (BNF).

Group 1: notify the DVLA if insulin treatment will last more than 3 months; check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; if it is 5.0 mmol/L or less, eat a snack first; do not drive if glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L. Group 2 has stricter rules.
NICE NG17: structured education (for example DAFNE) 6–12 months after diagnosis, offer of continuous glucose monitoring, and ongoing specialist care.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Believed him from the first minute; asked how he felt now before exploring; set a clear agenda on the phone.
Stopped eating with his family; blame from relatives; self-restriction; drives for work.
Picked up “fruity breath” and nausea, the weight loss in a slim man, and “it must be me”.
Idea (he caused it by eating wrong), concern (shame, relentless weight loss), expectation (stronger tablets or to be told what he is doing wrong).
Capillary glucose and blood ketones today; same-day diabetes team or acute assessment; GAD antibodies and C-peptide to confirm type, without delaying insulin (NICE NG17).
Type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes vs type 2; tested with age, BMI, weight loss, family and autoimmune history and viral prodrome.
Screened for DKA features (vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, breathlessness, ketotic breath); low threshold for admission.
Stated: likely autoimmune (type 1) diabetes misclassified as type 2, with possible ketosis — not his fault.
Seen within the hour; specialist contacted; insulin anticipated; no extra oral agents; stop dietary restriction; someone else drives him.
Asked about personal and family autoimmune disease; DVLA advice for insulin; interim medicines advice; family narrative addressed.
999 for vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or rapid breathing; nurse pre-warned; afternoon call-back; teach-back.

social.t: Relatives have framed the illness as his fault; he now eats alone and restricts food. Give him words to explain autoimmune diabetes at home and offer to see him with his wife.
He drives for work. Time off for admission and insulin starting, and a fit note if needed; later, a plan for glucose checks around driving.

legal.t: Group 1: notify if insulin will be needed for more than 3 months; glucose check within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; snack first at 5.0 mmol/L or less; do not drive below 4.0 mmol/L. Group 2 (lorry, bus) has additional requirements. Ask what he drives.
Insulin-treated diabetes may meet the definition of disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work, such as breaks for glucose checks and injections.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and the professional duty of candour: explain honestly that the original classification was probably wrong, without blaming colleagues, and record the revised working diagnosis and the plan.
A slim adult coded as type 2 on HbA1c alone, with no ketone check, is a learning opportunity for the practice: review how diabetes type is assigned at diagnosis.

community.t: Diabetes UK and Breakthrough T1D for newly diagnosed adults; structured education (for example DAFNE) via the diabetes team; peer support groups for adults diagnosed with type 1 later in life.

redFlags: Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, rapid or deep breathing — possible DKA, 999 or emergency admission
Ketotic (pear-drop) breath, nausea, marked thirst and polyuria with weight loss — same-day ketones and glucose
Slim, under 50, rapid failure of oral treatment, no family history of type 2 — suspect type 1 or latent autoimmune diabetes (NICE NG17)
psychosocial: Blame from family; eating alone; deliberate food restriction
Shame absorbed from the original diagnosis
Drives for work — licence and income worries
ice: Idea: “The tablets aren’t working because I’m eating wrong — it must be me.”
Concern: shame, family judgement and frightening weight loss
Expectation: stronger tablets, or to be told what he’s doing wrong

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable autoimmune (type 1) diabetes, possibly latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, misclassified as type 2: slim, 38, 6 kg weight loss, marked osmotic symptoms, rapid failure of metformin and gliclazide, no family history of type 2 diabetes, preceding viral illness. Symptoms suggest ketosis — DKA must be excluded today.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “I think your immune system has damaged the cells that make insulin. That’s a different kind of diabetes from the one you were told, and it isn’t caused by food. Without enough insulin your body burns itself for fuel — that’s the weight loss and the funny-smelling breath — and the fix is insulin.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been punishing yourself for something you didn’t cause. This isn’t about eating wrong, and stronger tablets won’t help — insulin will.”
management.psychosocial: Stop the food restriction today; give him the words for his family; offer a joint conversation with a family member if he wishes; address work and driving.
sharedPlan: Seen within the hour: capillary glucose and blood ketones; same-day diabetes team or acute medicine discussion
Insulin via the specialist team; GAD antibodies and C-peptide if the type remains uncertain (NICE NG17) — not delaying treatment
Eat normally, drink sugar-free fluids, no driving today, no self-adjustment of tablets
safetyNet: Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or rapid breathing — 999
Nurse pre-warned; GP call-back this afternoon; follow-up once the specialist plan is in place

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is in the title of his records: “type 2”. The station is failed by treating the label and passed by treating the patient — a slim young man in insulin deficiency who thinks it is his fault.

items.fail: Adding a third oral agent or advising stricter carbohydrate restriction.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG17 features point to type 1; insulin, not more tablets, is needed.
items.fix: Say you doubt the type 2 label and arrange same-day specialist input.

items.fail: Missing the ketotic breath and nausea.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Evolving DKA must be excluded today.
items.fix: Ask directly about vomiting, abdominal pain, breath and drowsiness; check ketones within the hour.

items.fail: Waiting for GAD antibodies before acting.
items.why: Antibodies help classify, but NICE NG17 treats type 1 as a clinical diagnosis; delay risks DKA.
items.fix: “We’ll do the antibody test, but we won’t wait for it to treat you.”

items.fail: Letting “my family say I’m sneaking food” pass.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The blame is the hidden agenda and is driving self-starvation.
items.fix: Say explicitly: “You didn’t cause this. It’s your immune system, not food.”

items.fail: Delivering the new diagnosis without acknowledging the earlier mislabelling.
items.why: He will not trust the new plan if the old one is defended.
items.fix: Be honest and non-blaming: “I think the first label was probably wrong.”

items.fail: Vague safety-netting and letting him drive himself in.
items.why: Non-specific advice in possible DKA is unsafe.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, arrange a driver, pre-warn the nurse and book a call-back.
